This ensures that the architecture is robust enough to handle varying compliance needs. For instance, if one country requires stricter segregation of duties (SoD) controls, that would inform the overall design.

Next, I would leverage the role mapping tool during the migration to identify and create derived roles that cater to specific country requirements. This allows for flexibility while maintaining a core set of roles. Each derived role would be tailored to meet local regulations, such as specific access controls for financial data in countries with stringent SOX-like regulations.

Testing validation is crucial. I would implement a parallel testing approach, utilizing SU53 access logs and GRC mock runs to ensure that the authorization settings are functioning as intended before go-live. This helps identify any gaps in compliance early on.

Finally, ongoing monitoring and periodic reviews would be essential to adapt to any regulatory changes. This architecture not only supports compliance but also ensures a scalable and maintainable authorization model across the multi-country landscape.

In designing the authorization architecture for a multi-country S/4HANA rollout, I would start by conducting a thorough analysis of the regulatory requirements for each country involved. This involves engaging with local compliance teams to understand specific access controls, data privacy laws, and segregation of duties (SoD) requirements.

Next, I would architect a flexible role design that accommodates these varying requirements. This could include creating a baseline set of global roles that align with common functions across all countries, while also developing country-specific roles that address unique regulatory needs. For instance, during a recent project for a Fortune 500 manufacturing client, I directed the authorization architecture for an S/4HANA transformation across 11 countries, ensuring that our role design was adaptable to local regulations while maintaining a cohesive governance framework.

I would also implement a robust SoD framework, ensuring that any potential conflicts are identified and mitigated through structured remediation processes. Regular audits and access reviews would be essential to validate compliance and adjust roles as regulations evolve. Finally, I would leverage SAP GRC tools to automate monitoring and reporting, ensuring ongoing adherence to both local and global standards.
